A programming language by Ian Zepp · MIT

A language your model writes
and you actually read.

Faber is a statically typed, compiled programming language. A model writes it against the surface it predicts most reliably. You read the same program back in your own language — English, Thai, Arabic — because the compiler renders it, not a translator. Then it compiles to whatever you need to run: Rust, a native binary, or a GPU shader.

Install Faber Five-minute tour
8 reader surfaces 7 compilation targets 99% corpus → Rust 96% corpus → LLVM Norma standard library, bundled

Everyone reads it in their own language

One program — a tagged union, sized numerics, a typed error channel, defaulted parameters, pattern matching and a glyph closure. Pick a tab and it is still that program. These are not translated comments or a localized tutorial; the compiler accepts every one of these spellings. Only keywords and type names change — identifiers and string literals stay exactly as written, so two people who share no language can still talk about satura on line one.

f main.fab · reader locale
faber format --reader-locale llm — the model-facing pack — what a model writes, and what an English reader reads today
union Pixel {
    Opacus {
        int<u8> nivea
    },
    Vitreus {
        int<u8> nivea
        f32 alpha
    },
    Vacuus,
}

fn satura(int datum, int meta optional coalesce 255) → int<u8> ⇥ string {
    if datum < 0 {
        throw format("sub limine: §", datum)
    }
    if datum > meta then return meta ↦ int<u8>
    return datum ↦ int<u8>
}

fn nomina(Pixel p) → string {
    match p {
        case Opacus const nivea {
            return format("opacus §", nivea)
        }
        case Vitreus const nivea, alpha {
            return format("vitreus § @ §", nivea, alpha)
        }
        case Vacuus {
            return "vacuus"
        }
    }
}

main {
    const (int) → int duplica ← int x ∴ x * 2
    do {
        const int<u8> v ← satura(duplica(150))
        print nomina(Opacus(v))
    }
    catch err {
        print format("erratum: §", err)
    }
}
faber format --reader-locale la — canonical Faber — the classical surface the language is named for
discretio Pixel {
    Opacus { numerus<u8> nivea },
    Vitreus { numerus<u8> nivea, fractus<f32> alpha },
    Vacuus
}

functio satura(numerus datum, numerus meta sponte vel 255) → numerus<u8> ⇥ textus {
    si datum < 0 ergo iace "sub limine: §"(datum)
    si datum > meta ergo redde meta ↦ numerus<u8>
    redde datum ↦ numerus<u8>
}

functio nomina(Pixel p) → textus {
    discerne p {
        casu Opacus fixum nivea { redde "opacus §"(nivea) }
        casu Vitreus fixum nivea, alpha { redde "vitreus § @ §"(nivea, alpha) }
        casu Vacuus { redde "vacuus" }
    }
}

incipit {
    fixum _ duplica ← numerus x ∴ x * 2
    fac {
        fixum numerus<u8> v ← satura(duplica(150))
        nota nomina(finge Opacus { nivea = v })
    }
    cape err {
        nota "erratum: §"(err)
    }
}

$ faber run --interpret app
opacus 255

A reviewer sets their locale once. Nobody presses a translate button, and no model sits in the middle guessing — this is the compiler's own rendering, so the program you approve is the program that ships.

It compiles to whatever has to run it

Same program again, pointed the other way. Every panel below is literal radix emit output — nothing here is hand-written or illustrative. LLVM IR comes straight off the MIR, so Faber reaches native code without passing through Rust, C, or any other source language.

WebAssembly is absent from these tabs on purpose. This program uses numerus<u8>, and the MIR-to-WASM backend does not yet accept sized numerics, so it fails closed rather than emitting something wrong. That is what the target matrix measures.

f main.fab → target
radix emit --target rust main.fab — primary backend — reviewable source, then a native binary
// Generated by radix - do not edit
// Requires the faber language-runtime crate (add to Cargo.toml):
//   faber = { path = "../faber" }  # adjust path for your layout

#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub enum Pixel {
    Opacus {
        nivea: u8,
    },
    Vitreus {
        nivea: u8,
        alpha: f32,
    },
    Vacuus,
}

fn satura(datum: i64, meta: i64) -> Result<u8, String> {
    if datum < 0 {
        return Err(format!("{}", format!("sub limine: {}", datum)));
    };
    if datum > meta {
        return Ok(meta as u8);
    };
    return Ok(datum as u8);
}

fn nomina(p: Pixel) -> String {
    match p {
        Pixel::Opacus { nivea } => {
            return format!("opacus {}", nivea);
        },
        Pixel::Vitreus { nivea, alpha } => {
            return format!("vitreus {} @ {}", nivea, faber::display_fractus(alpha));
        },
        Pixel::Vacuus => {
            return "vacuus".to_string();
        },
    };
}

fn main() {
    let duplica: fn(i64) -> i64 = |x| (i64::checked_mul(x, 2).expect("numerus overflow"));
    match { let ok: Result<(), String> = 'fac_result: {
    loop {
        let v: u8 = match satura(duplica(150), 255) { Ok(fac_value) => fac_value, Err(fac_err) => break 'fac_result Err(fac_err) };
        println!("{}", nomina(Pixel::Opacus { nivea: v }));
    break;
    }Ok(())
    }; ok } { Ok(ok) => ok, Err(err) => {
        let err = err;
        println!("{}", format!("erratum: {}", err));
        ()} };
}

// Generated by radix - do not edit

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
)

type Pixel interface {
    isPixel()
}

type Opacus struct {
    Nivea uint8
}
func (Opacus) isPixel() {}

type Vitreus struct {
    Nivea uint8
    Alpha float32
}
func (Vitreus) isPixel() {}

type Vacuus struct {
}
func (Vacuus) isPixel() {}

func satura(datum int, meta int) (uint8, error) {
    if (datum < 0) {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("%v", fmt.Sprintf("sub limine: %v", datum))
    }
    if (datum > meta) {
        return uint8(meta), nil
    }
    return uint8(datum), nil
}

func nomina(p Pixel) string {
    switch __radixCase := any(p).(type) {
        case Opacus:
            nivea := __radixCase.Nivea
            {
                return fmt.Sprintf("opacus %v", nivea)
            }
        case Vitreus:
            nivea := __radixCase.Nivea
            alpha := __radixCase.Alpha
            {
                return fmt.Sprintf("vitreus %v @ %v", nivea, func(v float64) string { s := strconv.FormatFloat(v, 'f', -1, 64); if !strings.ContainsAny(s, ".eE") { return s + ".0" }; return s }(float64(alpha)))
            }
        case Vacuus:
            {
                return "vacuus"
            }
        default:
            panic("non-exhaustive discerne")
    }
}

func main() {
    duplica := func(x int) int { return func() int { left := x; right := 2; max := int(^uint(0) >> 1); min := -max - 1; if (left > 0 && ((right > 0 && left > max/right) || (right < 0 && right < min/left))) || (left < 0 && ((right > 0 && left < min/right) || (right < 0 && left < max/right))) { panic("numerus overflow") }; return left * right }() }
    faberErr0 := func() error {
        v, err := satura(duplica(150), 255)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Println(nomina(Opacus{Nivea: v}))
        return nil
    }()
    if faberErr0 != nil {
        err := faberErr0
        fmt.Printf("erratum: %v\n", err)
    }
}

// … 116 lines of generated display/runtime shim elided …

function satura(datum: number, meta: number = 255): FaberResult<number, string> {
    if ((datum < 0)) {
        return { ok: false as const, error: `sub limine: ${datum}` };
    }
    if ((datum > meta)) {
        return { ok: true as const, value: meta };
    }
    return { ok: true as const, value: datum };
}
function nomina(p: Pixel): string {
    {
        let t37: Pixel = ((value: Pixel): Pixel => value)(p);
        if (t37.tag === "Opacus") {
            const nivea = t37.nivea;
            return `opacus ${nivea}`;
        }
        else if (t37.tag === "Vitreus") {
            const nivea = t37.nivea;
            const alpha = t37.alpha;
            return `vitreus ${nivea} @ ${alpha}`;
        }
        else if (t37.tag === "Vacuus") {
            return "vacuus";
        }
        else {
            throw new Error("non-exhaustive discerne");
        }}
}
(() => {
    {
        const duplica: (p1: number) => number = (x: number) => (x * 2);
        const t64: FaberResult<any, string> = (() => { const t46 = satura(duplica(150));
        if (!t46.ok) {
            return { ok: false as const, error: t46.error };
        }
        const v: number = t46.value;
         console.log(__faberDisplay(nomina(Opacus(v)), "textus"));
         return { ok: true as const, value: undefined }; })();
        if (!t64.ok) {
            const err = t64.error;
            {
                console.log(__faberDisplay(`erratum: ${err}`, "textus"));
            }}
    }})();

The same core reaches the GPU

A function marked @ nucleum is a compute kernel. It is ordinary Faber — the annotation only says where it runs. This one is a matrix multiply: 

@ nucleum
functio multiplico(tf32[16, 8] a, tf32[8, 16] b, tf32[16, 16] out, u32 id) → vacuum {
    fixum tf32[16, 16] c ← a.matmul(b)
}

Four lines become a tiled matmul: 34 lines of WGSL and 36 of Metal, each with threadgroup shared memory, an 8×8 workgroup, a K-tile loop, out-of-bounds zero fill, two barriers and a bounds-guarded write. None of that is in the source. And the two dialects share almost nothing — WGSL wants var<workgroup> arrays, @group/@binding storage and workgroupBarrier(); Metal wants threadgroup float[], [[buffer(n)]] attributes and threadgroup_barrier().

f kernel.fab → GPU
radix emit --target wgsl-text kernel.fab — WebGPU compute shader
// Generated by radix wgsl-text (supported-with-limitations compute source).

var<workgroup> shared_a: array<f32, 64u>;
var<workgroup> shared_b: array<f32, 64u>;

@group(0) @binding(0) var<storage, read> a_in: array<f32>;
@group(0) @binding(1) var<storage, read> b_in: array<f32>;
@group(0) @binding(2) var<storage, read_write> output: array<f32>;

@compute @workgroup_size(8, 8, 1)
fn multiplico(@builtin(global_invocation_id) id: vec3<u32>, @builtin(local_invocation_id) local_id: vec3<u32>) {
  let i: u32 = id.x;
var acc: f32 = 0.0;
let row = id.y;
let col = id.x;
let ty = local_id.y;
let tx = local_id.x;
for (var k_tile: u32 = 0u; k_tile < 1u; k_tile++) {
    let k_start = k_tile * 8u;
    let a_idx = row * 8u + (k_start + tx);
    if (a_idx < 16u * 8u) { shared_a[ty * 8u + tx] = a_in[a_idx]; }
    if (a_idx >= 16u * 8u) { shared_a[ty * 8u + tx] = 0.0; }
    let b_idx = (k_start + ty) * 16u + col;
    if (b_idx < 8u * 16u) { shared_b[ty * 8u + tx] = b_in[b_idx]; }
    if (b_idx >= 8u * 16u) { shared_b[ty * 8u + tx] = 0.0; }
    workgroupBarrier();
    for (var kk: u32 = 0u; kk < 8u; kk++) {
        acc += shared_a[ty * 8u + kk] * shared_b[kk * 8u + tx];
    }
    workgroupBarrier();
}
let out_idx = row * 16u + col;
if (row < 16u && col < 16u) { output[out_idx] = acc; }
}
radix emit --target metal-text kernel.fab — Apple GPU compute shader
// Generated by radix metal-text (supported-with-limitations compute source).
#include <metal_stdlib>
using namespace metal;

kernel void multiplico(
    device const float* a_in [[buffer(0)]],
    device const float* b_in [[buffer(1)]],
    device float* output [[buffer(2)]],
    uint3 id [[thread_position_in_grid]],
    uint3 local_id [[thread_position_in_threadgroup]]
) {
    uint i = id.x;
threadgroup float shared_a[64];
threadgroup float shared_b[64];
float acc = 0.0;
uint row = id.y;
uint col = id.x;
uint ty = local_id.y;
uint tx = local_id.x;
for (uint k_tile = 0u; k_tile < 1u; k_tile++) {
    uint k_start = k_tile * 8u;
    uint a_idx = row * 8u + (k_start + tx);
    if (a_idx < 16u * 8u) { shared_a[ty * 8u + tx] = a_in[a_idx]; }
    if (a_idx >= 16u * 8u) { shared_a[ty * 8u + tx] = 0.0; }
    uint b_idx = (k_start + ty) * 16u + col;
    if (b_idx < 8u * 16u) { shared_b[ty * 8u + tx] = b_in[b_idx]; }
    if (b_idx >= 8u * 16u) { shared_b[ty * 8u + tx] = 0.0; }
    threadgroup_barrier(mem_flags::mem_threadgroup);
    for (uint kk = 0u; kk < 8u; kk++) {
        acc += shared_a[ty * 8u + kk] * shared_b[kk * 8u + tx];
    }
    threadgroup_barrier(mem_flags::mem_threadgroup);
}
uint out_idx = row * 16u + col;
if (row < 16u && col < 16u) { output[out_idx] = acc; }
}

And it runs

Triga is a graphics and geometry engine written in Faber. These frames were produced by Faber source compiled to WGSL and executed on a GPU — no JavaScript, no three.js, no engine underneath doing the real work.

Fast enough to use like a script

Faber also runs with no build step. faber run --interpret takes source through parse, typecheck and MIR lowering, then steps the MIR in-process — no rustc, no linker, no build directory.

Same program, end to end, median of 15 runs (M-series Mac)
CommandWall clock
faber run --interpret (incl. full typecheck)4.4 ms
python3 script.py (no typecheck)13.3 ms

Reproduce with the scripting docs. A statically typed language should not be slower to start than a dynamic one, and it isn't.
